newsitem.title: ITALY: EU toasts 40 amid defence row, EMU worries.
newsitem.headline: EU toasts 40 amid defence row, EMU worries.

text.p: The European Union toasted 40 years of increasing ties on Tuesday in a ceremony stirred by a spat over future defence policy and renewed questions about the fate of the bloc's single currency.

The two issues, both central to the future path of the European Union, intruded in Rome's Renaissance Campidoglio city hall, where EU foreign ministers and European dignitaries gathered to commemorate the bloc's founding Treaty of Rome.
The treaty was signed on March 25, 1957, creating the original six-country European Economic Community (EEC), forerunner of the 15-nation EU.

"Let us take inspiration...from the birth of the European Economic Community and build the Europe of the 21st century, a Europe for Europeans with Europeans," European Commission President Jacques Santer said.
"Life for the Union begins at 40," said Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU presidency.
Van Mierlo used the occasion to report to fellow ministers on progress towards a new EU treaty due to be sealed at a summit in Amsterdam in June.
He said progress had been made in fields from foreign policy to judicial affairs but other ministers suggested major work was still needed because of the depth of disagreement among member states.
The Dutch said a special ministerial meeting would be held on April 6 and 7 in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, to try to maintain momentum in the treaty talks.

France, Germany and Italy, seeking ever deeper ties, called for the creation of an EU defence structure by bringing the Western European Union into the bloc. But Britain and the EU's neutral states indicated they would have nothing to do with it.
"It is not part of the benefit of the (NATO) Atlantic Alliance to turn the European Union into an organisation for collective security," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said.
In Bonn, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, one of the most tenacious supporters of deeper integration, said the EEC had paved the way for decades of peace, freedom, prosperity and social security.

He coupled his praise with renewed insistence that European economic and monetary union (EMU) should start on time in 1999 on the basis of a rigorous reading of the single currency's guiding Maastricht Treaty.

Fresh doubts that countries, including Germany, can meet the tough budget deficit limits needed this year to join the euro were fuelled in Rome by a newspaper interview given by Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.

Dini, whose country is struggling to keep its deficit to within the crucial three percent of Gross Domestic Product, was quoted by business daily Il Sole 24 Ore as saying a one-year delay to the EMU start date would benefit all of Europe.
He insisted his remarks had been misinterpreted, saying an extra year would have been useful but that "Italy is not requesting a delay".
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said nothing had changed in his country's position. "Italy is ready and wants to enter from the start," he said.
But Prodi also took advantage of the ceremony to warn that the bloc must take action to curb its stubborn unemployment.
"When unemployment exceeds 10 percent as it does on the EU average, we are facing an unacceptable waste of human resources," Prodi said.
"It would be impossible to explain to our citizens that the world's greatest economic bloc was not capable of responding to their principal concern," he said.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, meanwhile, tied the single currency to the Treaty of Rome, signed by Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany. It went into force in 1958, creating a common market among nations that had fought both the century's world wars.
"The single currency will complete the journey begun in 1958. We are entering into a new period," de Charette said.
